The Persistence of Small Things

There is a particular quality to the light at four in the afternoon during late autumn that I have never been able to name. It is not the golden hour of photographers, nor the blue melancholy of dusk approaching. It exists in the narrow band between these states, when the sun has descended enough to cast long shadows but still retains enough warmth to make those shadows appear soft rather than severe. I have spent perhaps too many hours observing this light, watching it move across the floorboards of various apartments I have inhabited, noting how it catches dust particles in the air and transforms them into something almost magical, tiny galaxies suspended in the stillness of a room.

I mention this because I believe our lives are composed primarily of such unnameable moments, and that we have constructed elaborate systems of distraction precisely to avoid confronting this fact. We seek narrative arcs, climactic resolutions, definitive meanings. Yet existence proceeds mostly through accumulation rather than transformation. The person you were at twelve remains nested within the person you are at forty, not as a ghost or a discarded shell, but as a living layer, still active, still influencing currents you cannot fully perceive.

I remember being twelve and discovering that my father kept a collection of stones in a wooden box in his closet. This was a man who presented himself as entirely practical, a mechanical engineer who spoke of efficiency and measurable outcomes. The stones were not precious. They were not even particularly attractive by conventional standards. Some were river-smoothed, others jagged from recent fractures, a few bearing the imprint of fossils that required close inspection to identify. I asked him once, indirectly, about this collection. He mentioned that he had started it at my age, that each stone represented a place he had been alone. Not lonely, he clarified, though I suspect this distinction mattered more to him than he admitted. Alone, meaning without the social performances that even then were beginning to exhaust him.

The stones remained in that box until his death. I have them now, scattered across windowsills in my own apartment, where the four o'clock light finds them on certain days. I have added to the collection, though I am less systematic than he was. My stones tend to accumulate rather than be chosen. I find them in pockets of coats I haven't worn in seasons, or in the corners of bags I have carried through airports and forgotten to empty. They are not mementos in any deliberate sense. They are evidence of attention I must have paid at some moment, to some texture or color or weight, though I rarely remember the specific circumstances.

This is how I understand inheritance now. Not the transmission of values or wisdom or even trauma, though all of these occur. Rather, the continuation of certain modes of attention, certain quiet practices that require no justification and serve no obvious purpose. The stone collection is not a hobby. It has no audience, no improving function, no narrative I could tell about it that would interest anyone else. It is simply a way of being in the world that my father demonstrated and that I find myself, without decision, perpetuating.

I think often about the concept of attention as a moral quality. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I am less certain of its purity than she was, but I accept its rarity. Genuine attention—sustained, unproductive, directed toward something that offers no return—is difficult to maintain in an economy that monetizes every glance and click. We have learned to scan rather than to look, to assess utility quickly and move on. The stone in your pocket becomes merely a stone, an inconvenience, something to discard. It requires a different kind of engagement to allow it to remain, to let it persist as a weight against your thigh, a reminder of gravity and mass and the specific geology of wherever you happened to be when you bent to pick it up.

There is a bench in a park near where I live that faces a pond where herons sometimes fish in the early morning. I have sat on this bench perhaps two hundred times over five years. I have seen herons perhaps thirty of those times. The ratio does not matter to me, though I know it would to many. The expectation of herons is not why I go. I go because the bench is slightly damp in a particular way that I find pleasant, because the angle of the path creates a sightline where people appear suddenly from behind a curve of shrubbery and then disappear again, because the sound of traffic is muffled here by some accident of topography and the pond's small fountain provides a continuous white noise that I have come to need without fully understanding why.

On the bench, I have written nothing of consequence. I have read less than I intended to. Mostly I have sat, and the sitting has been the activity, though we lack a vocabulary to describe sitting as activity. We call it waiting, or resting, or killing time—all phrases that assume the presence of some more authentic engagement elsewhere, waiting to resume. I am not waiting for anything on that bench. If a heron appears, I watch it. If not, I watch the water's surface respond to wind, or the way light changes on the bark of a particular willow that leans at what seems an unsustainable angle but has maintained this posture for at least the five years I have been observing it.

The willow is, I believe, dying. This is not a dramatic process. Each year fewer leaves return to certain branches. The lean has increased by perhaps a degree. No one has intervened because the tree is not in a location where it threatens property, and because parks departments have limited resources and this tree is not remarkable by any standard criteria. I have thought about photographing it to document the change, but this would require a system, a schedule, a commitment to evidence that would alter the nature of my attention. I would become a witness rather than a companion. The tree would become data. So I have not photographed it, and I will not, and when it falls I will notice its absence before I remember to look for it, and then I will feel something for which I will also lack adequate words.

We are taught to value change, growth, development. The static is suspect, associated with stagnation, depression, failure. Yet I find myself increasingly drawn to what persists without improving, without story, without destination. The stones in their various locations. The bench and its dampness. The willow's slow decline. These are not symbols of anything. They do not stand in for larger truths about resilience or decay or the passage of time. To make them symbols would be to recruit them into the economy of meaning that they exist, for me, outside of.

I am aware that this sounds like a defense of mere aestheticism, or worse, a kind of privileged withdrawal from engagement with suffering and injustice. I do not think it is either, though I cannot fully defend against these readings. What I can say is that my attention to these small persistences has not diminished my capacity for other forms of attention, to other people's pain or to the political structures that produce it. If anything, the practice of sustained looking seems to have expanded my tolerance for complexity, my ability to hold multiple temporal scales simultaneously. The heron fishing is immediate, present, entirely without past or future in its own experience. The willo operates on decades. The stones in my father's collection span half a century and two generations. None of these scales is more real than the others. None can be translated into a common currency without loss.

I have been thinking lately about the concept of maintenance as opposed to creation. We celebrate creators, innovators, disruptors. We have few rituals for those who maintain—who keep the systems running, who repair what breaks, who remember the practices that do not need to change. A friend who works in water infrastructure tells me that the most critical personnel in any municipal system are not the engineers who design new plants but the operators who understand the specific quirks of the existing machinery, who can hear when a pump is beginning to fail, who have developed over decades an embodied knowledge of pressures and flows that cannot be fully documented or transferred. These operators are retiring now, and their knowledge is disappearing faster than it can be replaced by sensors and automated systems.

I hear in this a larger pattern. The attention I give to the afternoon light, to the stones, to the willow—these are forms of maintenance, not creation. I am not producing meaning or beauty or insight. I am keeping something alive, though I could not say precisely what. A capacity, perhaps. A way of being that does not rush toward conclusion. The light at four o'clock does not care whether I observe it. The stones do not know they are collected. The willow is indifferent to my concern. This is the point, or rather, this is what makes it not a point at all. The maintenance is not for them. It is for the part of me that recognizes in their persistence a kind of solidarity, a shared condition of being in time without fully understanding what that means.

I am writing this now in late October. The afternoon light has reached the desk where I work, and I can see dust moving in the air, and I am reminded of all the other rooms where I have watched similar dust in similar light, and how each of those moments seemed entirely singular and entirely repeatable, both at once. This is the paradox of attention: it makes the ordinary strange and the strange ordinary. The dust becomes remarkable because I am looking at it. The light becomes unnameable because I am trying to name it. The effort and its failure are not separate from the experience but constitutive of it.

My father's stones include one that I have come to understand was collected on a day I was present for, though I was too young to remember. We were at a beach on a lake, and he walked away from where my mother and I were building something in the sand, and he returned with this stone, gray-green, with a white vein running through it like a crack that sealed itself. I know this because my mother mentioned it once, years later, not as a significant moment but as an example of his tendency to wander off, to become absent in body even when present in location. She found it irritating. I find it moving, this need he had to mark solitude even within the context of family, to maintain some boundary of self that the stone could represent.

I have stones from days with my own children, collected while they were occupied with other things, while I stepped away from the performance of fatherhood to bend down and pick up something that caught my eye. They do not know about these stones. The stones are not secrets, exactly, but they are private, part of a self that exists alongside my paternal self without being identical to it. I do not know if my children will find these stones after my death, or if they will understand what they represent, or if they will simply dispose of them as meaningless clutter. This uncertainty does not bother me. The stones are not messages. They are not meant to communicate anything. They are simply evidence that I was alone in certain places, that I paid attention to certain textures and weights, that I carried something back with me as proof of having been there, though the proof is only for myself and barely even for that.

The light is moving now, climbing the wall, and soon it will reach the corner where the ceiling meets the window frame, and then it will be gone for the day, leaving a different quality of light that I could also describe but will not, because I have reached the limit of what I can say about these things without repeating myself, and because repetition is another form of maintenance, and because I have maintained this attention long enough for now, and because the dust is still moving, and because the stones are still heavy in their various locations, and because the willow is still leaning, and because I will go to the bench tomorrow or the next day, not expecting herons but open to them, not waiting for anything, not resting from anything, simply sitting in the dampness, simply being present, simply continuing a practice that requires no justification and offers no conclusion, that persists because it persists, that is its own reason and its own reward, that is small and unimportant and therefore, in some way I cannot fully articulate, necessary.
